lesson.text: Quick memory: what is the Ring of Fire? (A line of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean.) In science you mapped where they happen. Now: why they happen, and how people prepare.

Earth is like a peach: a thin crust (the skin), a thick mantle of hot rock that flows very slowly, and a metal core. The crust is cracked into plates that drift a few centimetres a year, as fast as your fingernails grow.

Most volcanoes and earthquakes happen where plates meet. Plates can pull apart, as under Iceland. They can push together, one sliding under the other, as along Japan and the Andes. Or they can scrape past each other, as in California.
Deep down, melted rock called magma gathers in a magma chamber. It rises up a vent and bursts out of the crater. Once it is outside, it is called lava. Ash and gas can shoot high into the sky.

An active volcano has erupted recently or may soon; a dormant one is sleeping but could wake; an extinct one will never erupt again, like Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh. In AD 79, Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii.

An earthquake happens when rocks along a crack called a fault slip suddenly. Waves of shaking spread out from the point underground; the place on the surface right above it is the epicentre. Seismometers measure the shaking.

People prepare: buildings with bendy frames and deep foundations, and earthquake drills. A kit holds water, a torch and first aid. Scientists watch volcanoes for shaking, swelling and gas. Ash makes rich soil for farms.
Try it in the world: build a volcano with a magma chamber, a vent and a crater. Near it, build a village with an escape road and a meeting point. Next: water on the move.

exercises.prompt: What is magma called when it comes out of a volcano?
exercises.hint: Underground it is magma; outside it has another name.
exercises.explain: Magma is melted rock underground; once it bursts out, it is called lava.

exercises.prompt: Where do most volcanoes and earthquakes happen?
choices: in the middle of every field
exercises.explain: Most happen where Earth's plates meet, like all around the Pacific Ocean.

exercises.prompt: An extinct volcano will never erupt again.
exercises.hint: What is the difference between sleeping and extinct?
exercises.explain: True: an extinct volcano is finished; a dormant one is only sleeping.

exercises.prompt: What should you do indoors when an earthquake starts?
choices: drop, cover under a table and hold on
exercises.explain: Drop, cover and hold on: get under a sturdy table, away from windows, until the shaking stops.

exercises.prompt: Put the journey of melted rock in order.
exercises.hint: Start deep down and end at the surface.
items: lava bursts out of the crater
exercises.explain: Rock melts, magma gathers in the chamber, rises up the vent, bursts out of the crater as lava, and cools into new rock.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Two are parts of a volcano, two are about earthquakes.
exercises.explain: Crater: the top opening. Vent: the pipe. Fault: a crack where rocks slip. Epicentre: the place on the surface above an earthquake.

exercises.prompt: What buried the Roman town of Pompeii in AD 79?
exercises.hint: Pompeii is in Italy, near a famous volcano.
exercises.explain: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79 and buried Pompeii in ash. Archaeologists have been digging it up for over 250 years.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a volcano word or an earthquake word?
exercises.hint: Which ones are about melted rock?
exercises.explain: Volcano: lava, crater and magma. Earthquake: fault, epicentre and aftershocks, the smaller quakes that follow.

exercises.prompt: Earth's plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
exercises.hint: Only a few centimetres a year.
exercises.explain: True: a few centimetres a year, far too slow to feel, but over millions of years it moves whole continents.

exercises.prompt: Why do so many people live near volcanoes?
exercises.hint: Think about farms on the slopes of a volcano.
choices: volcanic ash makes rich soil for farming
exercises.explain: Ash breaks down into rich soil, so farms do well. Hot rocks can also heat homes, as in Iceland.

exercises.prompt: Iceland sits where two plates pull apart. What happens there?
exercises.hint: What fills the crack when plates pull apart?
choices: magma rises into the gap: volcanoes
the land sinks into the sea
exercises.explain: As the plates pull apart, magma rises into the gap, so Iceland has many volcanoes and hot springs.

exercises.prompt: A plate moves about 5 cm a year. How far does it move in 100 years, in metres?
exercises.hint: Work out the centimetres first: 100 lots of 5 cm. Then remember that 100 cm make 1 m.

exercises.prompt: Scientists see a volcano swelling and shaking more. What should the town do?
exercises.hint: Remember the warning signs that scientists watch for.
choices: follow its plan: warn people and leave
exercises.explain: Swelling and shaking can mean magma is rising: the town warns people and moves them away by the planned roads.

exercises.prompt: Every earthquake happens where people live.
exercises.hint: Where are many of the plates' edges?
exercises.explain: False: many earthquakes happen under the sea or far from towns, and most are too small to feel.

exercises.prompt: An earthquake measuring 6 shakes about 10 times as hard as one measuring 5. How many times as hard does one measuring 7 shake as one measuring 5?
exercises.hint: Each step up the scale is 10 times more: two steps is 10 × 10.
exercises.explain: From 5 to 6 is 10 times; from 6 to 7 is 10 times more: 10 × 10 = 100 times.
